name: Qwen3.8-27B + Open WebUI — private ChatGPT-style coding assistant
description: A private ChatGPT-style workspace in your browser, backed by Qwen3.8-27B running on the GPU next to it. Open the service URL, create your account on the first visit, and chat — nothing to install locally and no third party sees the conversation. Qwen3.8-27B is the strongest open coder at its size: 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6, 73.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with a 262K-token native context that swallows a whole repository's worth of files in one conversation. It is also natively multimodal, so you can drop in a screenshot of a broken UI, a whiteboard photo or a stack trace captured off another screen. Thinking is on by default and graded — pass reasoning_effort of low, medium or xhigh per request, or turn it off entirely for quick answers. Tool calling is wired up with vLLM's qwen3_coder parser, so Open WebUI's tools and MCP connections work rather than coming back as unparsed text. HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER: one container, one payment. vLLM serves the model on 127.0.0.1 only — the raw OpenAI-compatible API is never published, so there is no unauthenticated endpoint to find — and Open WebUI is the single exposed port. Open WebUI is installed at first launch into an isolated virtualenv on your bucket, deliberately separate from vLLM's own Python so its dependency pins cannot break the inference server, and it runs pinned to the CPU so the entire GPU stays with the model. AT LAUNCH select a persistent-storage bucket. There is no pre-configured account: the first account created in the browser becomes the administrator, and Open WebUI then switches signup off by itself, so open the service URL and register as soon as it is Running — until you do, anyone holding the URL could claim the administrator account. Accounts created afterwards, if signup is re-enabled from the admin panel, land as pending and see nothing until approved. The bucket holds three things that make relaunching cheap and continuous: the 31 GB of model weights, the Open WebUI virtualenv, and Open WebUI's own database, so your chat history, prompts, settings and account all come back on the next launch with the same bucket. Without a bucket the container refuses to start rather than re-download everything and then throw your history away on stop. Ask for exactly ONE GPU: the model runs with tensor-parallel size 1 and cannot use a second card, which would simply be billed while idle.
outcome: Open a browser and chat with Qwen3.8-27B on your own GPU — history, settings and account persist across launches.

includes.name: Open WebUI — chat interface, accounts, chat history, tools/MCP

workflows.name: Weights and history bucket
workflows.description: Not a workflow. This entry exists so the launch wizard offers the bucket picker: nodes-dashboard gates that picker on workflows[].length > 0 (templateNeedsBucketPicker in src/services/template-launch.ts). The bucket holds the model weights, the Open WebUI virtualenv and Open WebUI's database — without it the container refuses to start. The graph is deliberately empty and the container ignores COMFY_WORKFLOW entirely. Delete this once the node exposes a declarative persistence field.

requiredResources.description: ONE CUDA GPU with at least 40 GB of VRAM. The model is 27.8 GB in FP8 and the launch script gives vLLM 90% of the card, so a 48 GB card leaves roughly 15 GB of paged KV cache — enough for the full 262K context in a single conversation — while a 141 GB H200 leaves about 97 GB and serves many long conversations at once. Open WebUI and its retrieval embedding model are pinned to the CPU on purpose, so nothing competes with the model for VRAM. Ask for one card and not several: the model runs tensor-parallel size 1, a single-GPU process cannot spill onto a second device, and the extra card would be billed while idle. Staying on one GPU also keeps this template clear of the node's multi-GPU gap, where service containers get Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm and no ipc=host.
